clips.text: Look at these four numbers: point two, point four, point six, point one. Ignore their exact sizes and rank them from smallest to largest. In their original positions, the ranks are two, three, four, one.
That is an order pattern. Two players choose different patterns, then watch the same stream of random numbers. After each new number, inspect the latest four. Whoever sees their pattern first wins.

Suppose the first player chooses two, three, four, one. Move its final symbol to the front. You get one, two, three, four: an increasing run. This right rotation is a winning reply, even though both patterns are equally likely in one isolated window.

Here is a concrete stream. The first four values increase, so the rotation wins immediately. If we continued, the next window would have order two, three, four, one. The original pattern arrives one draw too late.

The theorem applies to independent observations drawn from one common continuous distribution. Independence means previous draws do not affect the next draw. Continuity rules out ties with probability one. We compare relative order, not particular numerical values.

Four distinct independent draws have twenty-four equally likely orders. Each chosen pattern has probability one over twenty-four in a single window. But neighbouring windows share three observations. Equal snapshot probabilities do not make the race fair.

Let us examine that shared information. Call our five observations x zero through x four. An increasing window first requires x zero below x one, below x two, below x three. The next window must place x four below x one to match the original pattern.

So x zero and x four both lie below the same chain of three values. Only their order relative to each other is undecided. There are exactly two compatible total orders. Watch the two bottom values exchange places.

Two increasing windows in a row have only one compatible order: all five values must increase. Starting with the original pattern cannot immediately produce either chosen pattern here, because the shared comparisons would have to rise and fall at once.

There are five factorial, or one hundred and twenty, equally likely orders of five draws. The signed overlap comparison gives two minus one, divided by one hundred and twenty. This is one local contribution. It is not the final winning probability or the final winning advantage.

For every pattern of length k, the corresponding one-position overlap contributes at least one over k plus one factorial. That gives the proof a positive starting amount. But all longer overlaps still need to be included before we can conclude anything about the race.

Why are some contributions added and others subtracted? Start with a counting example. Six objects have one property and five have another, with two objects in both groups. Six plus five counts those two twice, so subtract two to get nine different objects.

This is inclusion and exclusion. With more events, subtract double overlaps and add triple overlaps back. For the race, mark possible occurrences along the stream and alternate signs. A chain of overlapping marked occurrences is called a cluster.

Here are three consecutive occurrence starts. A cluster can mark only the first and last, giving a plus sign. Or it can mark all three, giving a minus sign. For a sequence satisfying both descriptions, those contributions cancel exactly.

The paper proves a recurrence for this cancellation. For each new occurrence, add the earlier surviving coefficients less than k starts away, then change the sign. Starting at minus one, the only possible coefficients are minus one, zero and plus one.

For length four with an occurrence at every start, the coefficients begin minus one, plus one, zero, zero, minus one, plus one. Nonzero signs alternate. In any four consecutive start positions, at most two survive. This prevents the number of markings from overwhelming the bound.

There is another useful counting trick for short overlaps. Shared observations already have a fixed order. Between them, private observations form two ordered chains. Combining those chains means choosing how their blue and teal entries interleave.

With two entries of each colour, there are six interleavings. For a simple illustration, require the first entry to be blue. Three choices remain. Swapping blue and teal sends each allowed choice to a different, disallowed choice.

In the proof, differing private ranks impose unequal colour counts at a boundary between shared values. Swapping colours again produces a disjoint set. So at most half of all balanced interleavings are allowed. This bounds the short overlaps that could work against the rotation.

What about arbitrarily distant overlaps? Group actual occurrences into a clump whenever consecutive starts are less than k positions apart. Focus on the clump containing the occurrence at start zero. We need a bound on how far this particular clump can continue.

For length four, finish observing one anchor window, then look for another occurrence starting at least four positions later. To remain in the same clump, the next anchor must start within three candidate positions. Those candidate windows use observations fresh after the previous anchor ends.

Each candidate window has probability two over twenty-four of matching either pattern. Add the three probabilities to bound the chance of any match: at most one quarter. The candidate windows overlap each other. This is a union bound, not an assumption that they are independent.

In general, r is twice the quantity k minus one, divided by k factorial. Repeating the necessary condition gives powers of r. One quarter, one sixteenth, one sixty-four: these shrink fast. Adding the geometric series bounds everything beyond a chosen cutoff.

Only anchors that remain in the original clump are counted. New occurrences elsewhere in the endless stream do not extend that clump. Combined with the cancellation bound, this gives a rigorous limit on the entire omitted contribution, not just a guess from a long simulation.

The proof now separates pattern lengths. Three was already handled by Elizalde and Lin. Lengths four through seven use exact finite calculations with a proven tail bound. Every length at least eight is covered by one uniform written argument.

For the infinite range, scale the signed comparison so the initial positive contribution is at least one. Subtract bounds for all adverse short overlaps and the long tail. The remaining guaranteed margin is positive, about zero point zero nine five, for every length at least eight.

This margin is a scaled signed comparison, not a universal nine-point-five percent winning advantage. A proved first-occurrence identity turns its positive sign into the conclusion that the rotation wins more than half the races. The conversion factor is positive but depends on the patterns.

At the shorter lengths, count all compatible total orders up to a specified span, using integers. Then compare the exact partial sum with a bound on the whole remaining tail. If the positive partial sum is larger, no unseen contribution can reverse its sign.

For length four, the scaled partial sum is greater than three quarters, while the absolute tail is at most five twelfths. The gap is safely positive. The other three rows pass the same test. These are exact rational comparisons, not rounded simulation estimates.

There are two thousand, nine hundred and fifty-two representatives across lengths four through seven. Reflecting all ranks covers the other half of the patterns without changing the game. Python and C plus plus independently reconstructed every integer coefficient, and their outputs agree.

For length three, an extra check counts races through eighteen observations. Give every unresolved race to the original pattern, the worst possible assumption for the rotation. Even then, the original pattern wins with probability below forty-seven percent. This verifies a known case, with no novelty claim.

Put the ranges together. For every length at least three, and every starting permutation, moving the last symbol to the front produces a reply with winning probability strictly above one half. The result is specific to the independent continuous observation model.

Winning does not mean best. Another reply might have a larger advantage. This work does not find the optimal reply for every pattern or give every exact winning probability. The cluster method itself is prior work, credited in the paper.

Remember the mechanism: equal snapshots can have unequal arrival times, overlapping windows create a directional advantage, and cancellation plus tail bounds controls everything the small example leaves out. Correctness confidence is high. Originality confidence is moderate after a bounded search.

The paper, exact certificates and independent execution records accompany this video. The argument is computer assisted, not formalised in Lean. Valyu Research, 2026. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
